Here are the exact prompts I use to produce a full AI story video from idea to upload

These are the prompts running behind $2M+ in channel revenue across my community, far beyond any generic "write me a YouTube script" request. Every prompt is designed for Claude Opus 5, and nearly all of them work with any frontier model.

STAGE 1: niche research prompt (Claude + NexLev MCP)

"Use NexLev MCP to find 10 YouTube channels in the [NICHE] space launched in the last 12 months with average views above 1,000 per video. Return the channel name, subscriber count, total videos, average views per video, estimated RPM range, primary audience demographic, and the titles of the top 3 outlier videos for each channel. Sort by average views descending."

This prompt pulls live YouTube data through NexLev's MCP integration. The output is a structured research report replacing 2-3 hours of manual tab-opening. You get channel-level performance data, outlier titles, and RPM estimates in one response.

STAGE 2: outlier analysis prompt

"Analyze the outlier video titles from the channels above. Identify 1) the most common emotional triggers used in high-performing titles, 2) the structural formulas repeated across outliers (e.G. [person] + [action] + [nation]), 3) which title lengths perform best, 4) whether broad titles outperform specific titles. Based on the patterns, generate 15 title ideas optimized for outlier performance in this niche."

Feed this to Claude right after the niche research prompt. The model analyzes the patterns across all the outlier titles and reverse-engineers the formula driving clicks. The 15 title ideas at the end are data-backed rather than creative guesses.

STAGE 3: script generation prompt

"You are a professional long-form narrative scriptwriter for YouTube AI story channels. Write a [LENGTH]-minute voiceover script about [TOPIC] using the following structure:

HOOK (first 30 seconds): open with a specific date, location, and character. Establish immediate tension or stakes. The viewer must know within 30 seconds why this story matters.

CONTEXT (minutes 1-5): establish the wider context, the stakes beyond the individual story, and introduce the key characters with ONE specific, memorable anecdote per character establishing personality and motivation.

RISING CONFLICT (minutes 5-15): build tension through escalating events. Each scene raises the stakes. Alternate between high-intensity and breathing room. Never maintain the same intensity for more than 3 minutes.

CLIMAX (minutes 15-18): deliver the payoff the hook promised. Use visceral, visual language. Make the viewer feel present in the moment.

RESOLUTION + LEGACY (minutes 18-20): connect the story's outcome to something bigger. Show why this event mattered beyond itself. End with a line worth remembering.

RULES: skip filler phrases entirely, drop the "welcome to the channel" opener, and don't use rhetorical questions as transitions. Every sentence earns the next one. Use specific numbers, dates, names, and locations throughout. The script must be factually accurate."

This is the core scripting prompt. The structure embedded in the prompt holds Claude to a retention-optimized narrative arc instead of rambling through information at a flat pace. The rules section eliminates the AI-isms (filler, rhetorical transitions, generic openers) before they appear.

Adjust [LENGTH] and the minute ranges to match your niche's optimal video length.

STAGE 4: image generation prompt

"Based on the following script, generate 20 image generation prompts for [IMAGE MODEL, e.G. NanoBanana Pro] producing super-realistic images depicting key moments from the story. Each prompt should specify character age, physical appearance (clothing, hair, expression, posture), setting (location, time of day, weather, architecture), lighting (direction, color temperature, mood), and camera angle (wide shot, medium, close-up). Maintain visual consistency by describing recurring characters with the same physical details in every prompt."

Paste the full script above this prompt. Claude reads the narrative and generates 20 scene-specific image prompts. The level of detail in the prompt ensures the image model receives enough visual direction to produce cinematic-quality output.

STAGE 5: thumbnail generation prompt

"I need a thumbnail image prompt for a YouTube video titled '[VIDEO TITLE]' in the [NICHE] niche. The thumbnail should 1) feature [NUMBER] characters with specific, exaggerated facial expressions conveying [EMOTION], 2) be set in [SETTING] with [LIGHTING CONDITIONS], 3) leave the top corners relatively uncluttered for title text overlay, 4) use [COLOR TEMPERATURE] tones matching the mood. Style reference: hyperrealistic cinematic film still, 16:9 horizontal, [GENRE DESCRIPTOR]. Include 8k detail, photorealistic skin texture, volumetric light, and shallow depth of field."

Send this along with a competitor thumbnail as a style reference. Claude generates a prompt specific to your video and niche. The "leave top corners uncluttered" instruction is critical because you need space for the text overlay doing the emotional selling.

STAGE 6: channel description prompt

"Rewrite the following YouTube channel description to sound professional, engaging, and niche-appropriate for a [NICHE] channel. Keep the tone [TONE: mysterious/authoritative/warm]. Include a brief hook explaining what the channel covers, a line on upload frequency, and a subtle call to subscribe. Under 150 words."

Paste a competitor's description below the prompt. Claude rewrites the description matching the tone of your specific niche. Use the output as your channel description AND your default video description.

STAGE 7: translation prompt (for secondary language channels)

"You are a professional literary translator and localizer for long-form narrative video scripts. Translate the script below from english into [TARGET LANGUAGE]. Rules: 1) translate 1:1, faithful and complete. Do not summarize, shorten, expand, or omit anything. 2) preserve the original meaning, tone, emotional register, narrative voice, pacing, and rhythm. Translate idioms and expressions into natural equivalents. 3) localize character names and place names into natural forms for [TARGET LANGUAGE]. Keep names 100% consistent throughout. 4) preserve exact formatting and paragraph structure. 5) output ONLY the translated script, with no preamble or notes attached."

Translation channels multiply your revenue with minimal extra work. One script, two languages, two revenue streams. This prompt ensures the translated version reads like a native script rather than a Google-translate artifact.

NEW RESEARCH: You can now create a new robot optimized for any given task!

I love this new project by @haqhuy, @SongShuran, and others.

Called "Transformer Transformer: A Unified Model for Motion-Conditioned Robot Co-design", it generates a robot's physical design and its controller together from a task spec.

DEFINITIONS:
- Reward function: A scoring rule that assigns a number to how well a behavior achieves the task. Here, it is the objective the generated design is pushed to maximize (e.g., track the target motion with low error).
- Tokenizing: dividing continuous or structured data (a robot's links, joints, motor specs, states, actions) into a discrete vocabulary of symbols a transformer can process, the same step that turned pixels and audio into "language" for these models.
- Diffusion transformer (DiT): A transformer trained to turn random noise into structured output through iterative denoising. Here, it generates robot bodies and trajectories instead of images.
- MuJoCo: The standard fast physics simulator for robotics research (DeepMind-maintained). The Menagerie is its curated zoo of ready-to-use robot models.
- CMA-ES: Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy, the workhorse black-box optimizer: it evolves a population of candidate designs, keeps the best, and needs thousands of simulator rollouts.
- Bimanual multi-trajectory optimization: Finding one design/controller that performs well across several target motions for a two-armed robot at once, harder than optimizing for a single arm and a single motion.
- BERT/MAE masked-modeling trick: Train one model to fill in whatever parts of the input you hide (words for BERT, image patches for MAE); at inference, choosing what to mask chooses the task, so masking the body makes it a designer and masking the actions makes it a controller.

In practice, you give it a target end-effector motion and a reward function, and it outputs a complete embodiment (link, joint, motor, and inertial property), as well as a controller to drive it.

It works by tokenizing both the body (links/joints/motors) and the dynamics (states/actions) into a compact scheme called RoboTokens, training a diffusion transformer (DiT) over them.
The same model predicts dynamics using those predictions ("Dynamics Self-Guidance") to push generated designs toward higher reward at inference time.
Masking different token types (using the BERT/MAE masked-modeling trick) lets the one model do three jobs: generate an embodiment, control an arbitrary embodiment, or design one conditioned on a motion.

It is trained on 11 robots from the MuJoCo Menagerie (0.65 kg hand to 67.5 kg quadruped, 6–35 joints), and validated in sim and on a physical ALOHA doing cloth flinging.

I like the fact that this approach inverts the entire recent robotics ideas: designing a policy for a fixed robot -> designing the robot for a fixed task.
Every other approach assumes the body is given and learns a controller.
Transformer Transformer takes the task (target motion + reward), then generates the body and controller jointly.

In practice, it is a ~180× speedup over the standard optimizer at equal-or-better quality.
It reaches "CMA-ES-level quality in seconds" and finishes bimanual multi-trajectory optimization in <1 min vs CMA-ES's 3+ hours.

Surprisingly, this approach was validated on real hardware!
The generated design was measurably smoother.
On a physical ALOHA flinging cloth (a deformable, dynamic task), the optimized design cut tracking error 73% and peak joint speed 30% versus the original, with fewer joint-speed peaks.
Therefore: real world results, not a sim-only benchmark -> that is worth underlining nowadays!

Also worth mentioning: this is the lab behind UMI and Handroid, that I mentioned here previously!
The team seems extremely creative, i love these out-of-the-box approaches.

Example:

I've been working on this little notch app that has a few keyboard shortcuts.  I wanted to use established UI patterns to teach the user about those shortcuts w/o cluttering the UI, so...

1. I asked codex, something like:

"help me find a standard UI pattern to expose shortcuts to the user in a way that doesn't clutter the UI. try using image gen to generate a mockup first."

It responded with something like image 2.

2. I highlighted the suggested interaction convention text and clicked "more details"

This is magic.  What happens:

FIRST: codex app sends that annotation along with some context from your ongoing work thread to chat gpt (doesn't use you codex limits!). This opens the thread in a "quick chat" window with the context primed.

SECOND: I follow up with a new message like:

[pasted screenshot of the current UI]
"can you do research on this UI convention?"

It goes out to the web, discovers a bunch of sources on UI/UX patterns relevant to showing shortcuts to a user in a macOS app.  Gives me a crash course on the topic. Very cool.

THIRD: I then follow up with: "generate a mockup illustrating your suggested pattern(s)"

It then generates an image doing just that (image 3)

3. I click the "Add to Chat" button in the quick chat window header (image 4)

This little button re-injects the context from this quick chat thread (including the mockup image) back into the main Codex work thread (wtf!)

LAST: I follow up, back in the main chat now:

[Shortcut Discovery Design thread] review both suggested approaches (your own against the helper research thread) and decide on a best final approach.

This results in a final interaction pattern suggestion where it drops its own "hover-only keyboard icon" and in adopts portions of the external thread's researched pattern.

Then I follow up with "mockup pls"...

This Paper is one of the cleverest solutions I’ve seen for fixing Diffusion Alignment.

If you’ve worked with RLHF or Reward Backprop on DiTs, you must be tired of delayed feedback. 

Evaluating only the final image makes credit assignment a total nightmare. 

You either run out of VRAM trying to unroll the full trajectory, or you fight insane gradient variance with online RL.

The authors solve this by sticking learnable, position-free "register tokens" into a frozen DiT. 

Instead of waiting until step 50, these registers pull dense reward signals directly out of noisy intermediate latents. 

It turns out you can accurately judge trajectory quality surprisingly early in the denoising process.

What makes this paper stand out is how practical the applications are:

1-For training: Their distillation setup (RG-OPD) skips standard policy gradients entirely and hits the same alignment performance while using up to 33x fewer GPU hours. That’s huge for making alignment accessible.

2-For inference: You can use their Reward-Guided Sampling (RGS) to steer generation live off these register gradients thus improving both prompt adherence and visual quality without retraining or touching model weights.

It’s a super clean, well thought-out approach that addresses both the compute bottleneck and inference control at once. 

Definitely worth a read if you're working on generative models:
https://t.co/tfkSPmYwiU

Want to learn how to build a stunning AI fashion campagn using the new MiniMax-H3 Video model with open weights? Use this prompt below 👇

Minimax 3 Prompt: Create a premium 16:9 landscape fashion film. Use Image 1 for the overall mood, location, and film texture; Image 2 for the talent; Image 3 for the bag; and Image 4 for the closing brand mark. This is a fashion campaign for the clothing and bag. The tone is elevated, cool, and restrained, but the edit should still feel lively and fashion-forward—not like a conventional narrative film or an e-commerce ad.

Keep the story simple: beside a vintage car on a desert highway, a woman walks to the rear of the car, opens the trunk, takes out a black bag, shares a quiet beat with the man standing nearby, then leaves carrying the bag. Integrate the clothing and bag naturally into the performance so they feel like part of the characters’ identity.

I added the final video in and the reference images for you to learn from!
